quiz.q: You are −2% on the day against a 4% equity-based daily limit, with no trades open. What is the most you could risk on a new trade before any safety margin?
quiz.why: Remaining daily room = 4% − 2% − 0% open = 2%. In practice you would risk well under that to allow for spread and slippage.

quiz.q: On an account where the floor trails intraday equity, a trade reaches +2R open profit at 1% risk and then closes at entry. What happened to your buffer?
quiz.why: The floor rose with the open equity peak and did not come back down, so the distance to it shrank by roughly the open profit you gave back.

quiz.q: In the hypothetical simulation, what happened when a no-edge method increased risk from 1% to 3%?
quiz.why: Bigger risk resolves the challenge faster in both directions, turning it into a coin toss. It does not create an edge.

quiz.q: Two days before the deadline you are +5% against an 8% target. Which response fits a sound risk plan?
options: Risk 3% on the next setup to reach the target
Keep normal size and accept running out of time if necessary
Open several correlated trades at once
Remove stops to avoid the daily limit
quiz.why: Running out of time costs the fee. Oversizing risks a far more expensive failure and reinforces the worst habit in trading.

quiz.q: Which statement about the profit target is correct from a risk point of view?
options: It should set your risk per trade
It has no bearing on how much you should risk per trade
It should be divided by your number of trades to set risk
quiz.why: Risk is sized from the drawdown floor and your method's losing streaks. The target is a finish line, not a sizing input.

lessons.title: The Trade Journal and the Weekly Review
lessons.summary: Keep a trade journal in R that records rule adherence as well as results, and run a weekly and monthly review that tells you exactly what to fix.
lessons.html:
Every number in this course so far — win rate, average win, average loss, expectancy, streak length, drawdown — has to come from somewhere. That somewhere is your journal. Without one, your "edge" is a feeling, your risk rules are intentions, and every review is a conversation with your memory, which is the least reliable witness in trading.

This lesson shows you what to record, how to grade each trade, and how to run a short weekly review that turns a list of trades into a list of decisions.

What to record

Keep it short enough that you will actually fill it in — every trade, the same day. The essential fields:

Field Example Why it matters
Date, session 14 May, London Finds time-of-day patterns
Instrument, direction EUR/USD, long Exposure and pair-level stats
Setup name Trend pullback Stats per setup, not just overall
Entry, stop, target 1.0855 / 1.0830 / 1.0905 Defines planned R
Risk % and size 1%, 0.50 lots Proves sizing was calculated
Result in R (after costs) +2.0R The only result that is comparable
Rules followed? Yes / No (which rule) Separates skill from luck
Grade A / B / C Quality, independent of outcome
Note and screenshot "Clean HL, waited for close" What you saw, in your words, at the time

Optional but valuable: the furthest the trade went in your favour before closing (maximum favourable excursion, MFE) and against you (maximum adverse excursion, MAE), both in R. They tell you whether your stops and targets are well placed.

Grading: separate the decision from the outcome

Give every trade a grade for how well it followed your plan, not for whether it made money:

  • A — every rule followed: valid setup, correct size, stop and target as planned, managed as written.
  • B — valid setup, minor execution slip: early exit, late entry, small sizing error.
  • C — rule broken: no valid setup, oversized, stop moved away, revenge trade, limit ignored.

Then, every week, you can ask the two questions that matter: how did my A trades do? (that is your method) and what did my B and C trades cost? (that is your discipline).

Here are three journal screenshots from a hypothetical week.

KEY POINT

Grade the decision, not the outcome. A rule-following loss is an A; a rule-breaking win is a C.

The weekly review (30 minutes)

Once a week, at a fixed time and never on a trading day if you can avoid it:

  1. Count the trades and their grades. How many A, B and C?
  2. Score adherence. A trades as a percentage of all trades. This is your main weekly score — more important than P&L.
  3. Add up R by grade. Total R on A trades, and total R on B and C trades.
  4. Price the mistakes. For each B or C trade, write the difference between what the plan would have produced and what you actually got. That number is your cost of mistakes for the week.
  5. Check the limits. Were daily and weekly limits respected? Exposure caps?
  6. Write one change. One behaviour to work on next week — not a rule change, a behaviour.

Here is a hypothetical week, summarised:

Trade Grade Result Plan would have given Mistake cost
1 A +2.0R +2.0R —
2 A −1.0R −1.0R —
3 B +0.5R +2.0R −1.5R
4 A −1.0R −1.0R —
5 C −1.6R −1.0R −0.6R
6 C −1.0R 0R (no valid setup) −1.0R
7 A +2.0R +2.0R —
Total 4 A / 1 B / 2 C −0.1R +3.0R −3.1R

The week finished slightly negative. The A trades alone made +2R. The plan, followed perfectly, would have made +3R. Discipline cost 3.1R — more than the entire result. This trader does not need a new strategy. They need to fix three behaviours, and the journal has named every one of them.

COMMON MISTAKE

Reviewing only the P&L. A red week of A-grade trades is a good week: you executed, and variance did the rest. A green week full of C trades is a warning — it rewarded habits that will eventually cost you far more.

The monthly review

Once a month, with at least 30 trades in the sample where possible, step back and calculate the numbers from lesson 4 — separately for A-grade trades and for all trades:

  • Win rate, average win, average loss, expectancy in R.
  • Results by setup, by instrument and by session.
  • Longest losing streak and maximum drawdown against your plan's expectations.

The gap between "A-grade expectancy" and "all-trade expectancy" is the clearest measure of what your discipline is worth. If A-grade expectancy itself is negative over a large sample, the method — not your execution — needs work, and that is a decision for a calm review, not a Tuesday afternoon.

Making the journal stick

Most journals die in the third week. They start detailed and enthusiastic, become a chore, and quietly stop — usually during a losing run, which is exactly when the record is most valuable. A few habits keep them alive.

Log before you look at the result. Fill in the plan fields — setup, entry, stop, target, size, risk, grade of the setup — at the moment you place the order. Then the only thing left to add later is the outcome. A journal written after the result is always coloured by it: losing trades are suddenly remembered as "marginal setups" and winners as "obvious".

Take two screenshots. One at entry, with your levels drawn on the chart. One at exit. Together they show what you knew at the time and what happened next, and they stop hindsight from rewriting the story.

Keep the format fixed. A simple spreadsheet with one row per trade is enough. Add three formula cells at the top — total R, win rate and expectancy (sum of R divided by number of trades) — and the monthly review almost writes itself.

Never skip the bad days. A journal that only contains the trades you are comfortable recording measures nothing. The C-grade trades are the most important rows in the file, because they are the ones that tell you what to fix.

Review in R, talk in R. When you describe your week to yourself or to anyone else, use R and adherence, not pounds. "Five A trades, one C, +2.3R, mistake cost 0.8R" is information. "Up £230" is a mood.

Going deeper

MFE and MAE. If you record how far each trade went for you (MFE) and against you (MAE) before closing, patterns appear. If many losing trades reached +1.5R before reversing, your targets may be too far for the method, or a partial-profit rule may be worth testing. If many winners first went to −0.9R, your stops are about right; if almost none went beyond −0.4R, your stops might be wider than needed — test a tighter one on paper first.

Tagging emotions. A one-word emotional tag at entry — calm, rushed, bored, frustrated, confident — often explains more C-grade trades than any market factor. Most traders find their C trades cluster around one or two states. Those states become warning lights in the risk plan.

Change control. When the review suggests a rule change, write it down with the date and the reason, test it on a meaningful sample (paper, minimum size or replay), and only then adopt it. Never change a rule during a drawdown or on a trading day. The history of your rule changes is itself useful: if you keep loosening the same rule, that is where your edge is leaking.

THE RULES
  • Log every trade the same day, in R after costs, with a grade for rule adherence.
  • Grade the decision, not the outcome.
  • Run a 30-minute weekly review: adherence score, R by grade, cost of mistakes, one behaviour to fix.
  • Run a monthly statistical review; compare A-grade expectancy with all-trade expectancy.
  • Change rules only through a written, dated, tested process — never during a drawdown.

Summary

  • The journal is where every risk number in this course comes from; record each trade in R with its rule-adherence grade.
  • Grade A, B or C on decisions, not outcomes, so you can separate the method from your discipline.
  • The weekly review prices your mistakes in R and picks one behaviour to fix.
  • The monthly review compares A-grade expectancy with all trades; MFE and MAE refine stops and targets on evidence.

quiz.q: A trade followed every rule and lost 1R. What grade does it get?
options: A, because every rule was followed
No grade — losing trades are not graded
quiz.why: The grade measures adherence to the plan, not the outcome.

quiz.q: A trader took a trade with no valid setup and it made +2R. How should it be graded?
options: B — it was only a small error
quiz.why: A rule-breaking win is still a rule break. Logging it as an A would reward the habit.

quiz.q: In the hypothetical week, what did the B and C trades cost compared with following the plan?
quiz.why: The plan would have produced +3.0R; the actual result was −0.1R. The difference, −3.1R, is the cost of the mistakes.

quiz.q: Which is the main score for a weekly review?
options: Rule adherence — the share of A-grade trades
quiz.why: Adherence is what you control. Profit over a week is dominated by variance.

quiz.q: Many of your losing trades reached +1.5R before reversing to the stop. What is a sensible response?
options: Test a closer target or a partial-profit rule on a meaningful sample
Double risk on the next trade
quiz.why: MFE suggests the targets may be too far for this method. The right response is a tested, documented change, not an instant rule edit.

quiz.q: When should a rule in your risk plan be changed?
options: During a drawdown, to stop the losses
After a written, dated, tested review — never during a drawdown
Whenever a new strategy video suggests it
quiz.why: Rules changed in the heat of losses reflect mood, not evidence. Change control keeps the plan honest.

lessons.title: Capstone — Your Written Risk Plan
lessons.summary: Write a complete one-page risk plan, run the full pre-trade routine on three worked trades, and apply the plan when the answer is 'no trade'.
lessons.html:
Everything in this course now comes together into one document: a written risk plan. Not a manifesto and not a list of good intentions — a single page of numbers and rules that governs every trade you take, drafted while you are calm, so that no decision that matters is ever made while you are emotional.

The writing matters. An unwritten rule is a preference, and lessons 5 and 6 showed what happens to preferences under pressure: they get negotiated. A written rule can still be broken, but it cannot be quietly blurred. The breach is visible, it goes in the journal, and it can be fixed.

This lesson gives you the template, the step-by-step routine, three fully worked trades (one of them a loser), a final drill, the passport and the complete checklist.

The eight sections of the plan

Your plan answers eight questions, a sentence or two each. The answers below are illustrative — yours must come from your own testing, tolerance and journal.

1. Risk per trade. "1% of current balance, measured to the stop. 0.5% while in a drawdown of 10% or more from the equity peak." (Lessons 1 and 6.)

2. Sizing procedure. "Stop placed first by analysis. Size = money at risk ÷ (stop pips × pip value per lot), converted to GBP, rounded down, reverse-checked before entry. Spread added to stops under 15 pips." (Lesson 2.)

3. Minimum trade quality. "Only setups from my tested playbook. Stop at a genuine invalidation level; honest first target of at least 1.5R. Otherwise, no trade." (Lesson 3.)

4. Exposure caps. "Max 2% risk on any one currency. Max 5% total open risk. A second trade on the same theme at half size." (Lesson 7.)

5. Loss limits. "Daily −3R: platform closed. Weekly −6R: stop until Monday. −10% from equity peak: pause, formal review, half risk until half the drawdown is recovered." (Lesson 6.)

6. Stop and exit discipline. "Hard stop at the broker on every trade, placed with the order. Stops move only towards the trade. Exit by the written rule only. No holding through high-impact releases on my traded currencies." (Lessons 3, 4 and 6.)

7. Journal and review. "Every trade logged the same day in R after costs, with grade and emotional tag. Weekly 30-minute review on Saturday; monthly statistical review." (Lesson 9.)

8. Breach protocol. "Any broken rule: close the position if still open, log the breach, stop trading for the day. Three breaches in a month: next month at 0.5% risk." (Because a plan without consequences is a poster.)

KEY POINT

If a rule is not written down with a number in it, it is not a rule yet.

The pre-trade routine, step by step

This is the playbook. Every trade, every time, in this order:

  1. Status check. Am I inside my daily and weekly limits? Am I in a drawdown that changes my risk percentage? Any breach today?
  2. Setup check. Is this a setup from my written playbook, on a chart I would be happy to show in my journal?
  3. Stop. Where is the idea wrong? Place the stop there, plus a buffer for spread.
  4. Target. Where can price realistically go? Is the honest first target at least my minimum R?
  5. Exposure. Break the trade into currencies. Does it fit the per-currency and total caps? If it is a second trade on a theme, halve it.
  6. Size. Money at risk ÷ (stop pips × pip value), in one currency, rounded down. Reverse-check.
  7. Event check. Any high-impact release on either currency before the trade is likely to resolve?
  8. Enter with the stop attached. Log the plan fields immediately.

Any "no" ends the process. Flat is a position.

Worked trade 1 — EUR/USD long (winner)

Status: balance £10,000, no drawdown, no trades today. Risk 1% = £100.

  • Setup: trend pullback; higher low held; bullish confirmation close. Valid.
  • Stop: 20 pips, beneath the higher low (1.0894 entry, 1.0874 stop).
  • Target: 40 pips (1.0934), 2R. Still about 20 pips below the prior high, so the market has clear room to get there. Passes the 1.5R minimum.
  • Exposure: no open trades. EUR +1%, USD −1%. Inside caps.
  • Size: £100 × 1.2500 = $125. $125 ÷ (20 × $10) = 0.625 → 0.62 lots. Reverse check: 0.62 × $10 × 20 = $124 = £99.20. ✔
  • Events: none scheduled on EUR or USD before the likely resolution.
  • Result: target hit. +$248 = about +£198, logged as +2.0R, grade A. Balance ≈ £10,198.

Worked trade 2 — USD/JPY short (loser)

Status: balance £10,198; inside all limits. Risk 1% = £101.98.

  • Setup: downtrend; lower high; bearish close. Valid.
  • Stop: 35 pips above entry (150.80 entry, 151.15 stop), beyond the lower high plus spread buffer.
  • Target: 70 pips (150.10) at the prior low area, 2R.
  • Exposure: no other open trades. USD −1%, JPY +1%. Inside caps.
  • Size: £101.98 × 187.50 (illustrative GBP/JPY) = ¥19,121. ¥19,121 ÷ (35 × ¥1,000) = 0.546 → 0.54 lots. Reverse check: 0.54 × ¥1,000 × 35 = ¥18,900 = £100.80. ✔
  • Result: stopped out. −1.0R, grade A. Balance ≈ £10,097.

Note what did not happen. The stop was not moved. The next trade was not doubled to recover it. The journal entry says "valid short, failed; no action required". This is what a loss looks like inside a plan.

Worked trade 3 — XAU/USD long at half size (exposure rule)

Status: balance £10,097. A new EUR/USD long is already open at 1% risk, stop at its original level. Gold now offers a valid long.

  • Setup: uptrend; pullback into demand; bullish close. Valid.
  • Stop: $8.00 below entry ($2,361.00 entry, $2,353.00 stop), beneath the demand zone.
  • Target: $16.00 ($2,377.00), 2R.
  • Exposure: EUR/USD long (USD −1%) + gold long (USD −1% at full size) = USD −2%, on the cap, and a second expression of the same short-dollar theme. Rule: half size, 0.5% → USD −1.5%.
  • Size: 0.5% × £10,097 = £50.49 × 1.2500 = $63.11. $63.11 ÷ ($8 × 100 oz) = 0.079 → 0.07 lots. Reverse check: 0.07 × 100 × $8 = $56 = £44.80. ✔
  • Result: target hit. +$112 ≈ +£90, logged as +2.0R, grade A.

The R is the same as trade 1. The money is less, deliberately, because the account's real exposure was larger than the single chart suggested.

Practice drill — trade or no trade?

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the plan as a default that can be overridden by a "really good" setup. The plan's value is that it is not negotiable in the moment. The day you override it for a great setup is the day it stops being a plan.

Making it stick

Keep it in sight. Print the one page and put it beside the screen. Its job is to be in your eye-line at the moment you are tempted.

Review weekly, revise rarely. Re-read it every week. Amend it at most monthly, in writing, with a dated reason — and never on a trading day or during a drawdown.

Grade adherence before profit. A week of full adherence with a red P&L is a good week. Enough of those, and the P&L settles to whatever your edge honestly is — which is all anyone can ask.

Going deeper

Scaling the plan. As your journal grows, the plan can evolve on evidence: a different risk percentage for a setup with a long, stable record, a tighter daily limit for a high-frequency method, a stricter rule for a session where your C grades cluster. Each change follows the change-control process from lesson 9.

Plans for different accounts. If you trade a personal account and a prop-firm challenge, write a plan for each. The challenge plan's limits sit inside the firm's limits (lesson 8), and the two accounts' exposures should be considered together if you trade the same ideas in both.

The plan is the strategy. Markets will always be uncertain. Your risk is the one variable you fully control, and controlling it is what allows every other skill you learn to compound instead of resetting to zero.

THE RULES
  • Every trade passes the eight-step pre-trade routine; any 'no' means no trade.
  • Risk per trade, exposure caps and loss limits are written with numbers and never changed during a drawdown or on a trading day.
  • Any rule breach: close if open, log it, stop for the day.
  • Grade adherence before profit, every week.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • I am inside my daily, weekly and peak-drawdown limits, and my risk % reflects any drawdown rule
  • This setup is in my written playbook and I would be happy to show it in my journal
  • My stop is at the point where the idea is wrong, plus a spread buffer
  • My honest first target is at least my minimum R
  • I have broken the trade into currencies and it fits my per-currency and total caps (half size if it repeats a theme)
  • Size is calculated from the formula, converted to my account currency, rounded down and reverse-checked
  • No high-impact release on either currency before the trade is likely to resolve
  • The stop is attached to the order at the broker
  • The plan fields are logged in my journal before I look at the result

Summary

  • A written risk plan answers eight questions: risk per trade, sizing, trade quality, exposure, loss limits, stop and exit discipline, journalling and breach protocol.
  • The eight-step pre-trade routine turns the plan into yes/no questions; any 'no' ends the process.
  • Worked trades: +2R on EUR/USD at 0.62 lots; −1R on USD/JPY at 0.54 lots, handled without drama; +2R on gold at half size because of dollar exposure.
  • When a limit is hit, even a perfect setup is no trade.

quiz.q: Which comes first in the pre-trade routine?
options: Checking you are inside your loss limits and current risk level
quiz.why: If a limit is hit or a drawdown rule applies, nothing else matters — the status check comes before any analysis.

quiz.q: In worked trade 2, after the −1R loss, what did the plan require?
options: Double size on the next trade
Nothing beyond logging it — the trade was valid and the loss was as planned
quiz.why: A rule-following −1R loss is part of the method. The plan's response is to log it and carry on within the limits.

quiz.q: Why was worked trade 3 taken at 0.5% rather than 1%?
options: Gold is always traded at half size
It was a second short-dollar trade alongside an open EUR/USD long
The account was in a 10% drawdown
quiz.why: Long gold and long EUR/USD both sell the dollar. The exposure rule halves the second trade on the same theme.

quiz.q: You are at −3R for the day with a −3R daily limit, and an excellent setup appears. What does the plan say?
options: Take it — quality overrides the limit
No trade; the platform is closed for the day
Take it on a demo and copy it live if it works
quiz.why: The limit is not negotiable in the moment. That is the whole point of writing it down.

quiz.q: Using £10,000 at 1% and GBP/USD 1.2500, what is the correct size for a 20-pip EUR/USD stop?
When should the written risk plan be amended?
options: During a drawdown, to stop losses quickly
At most monthly, in writing with a dated reason, never on a trading day or in a drawdown
quiz.why: Plans should evolve on evidence through a calm, documented process — not in reaction to recent results.
